resident.chief_complaint: Progressive difficulty walking, declining balance, and neuropathic pain in the extremities for one year.
resident.history: A 63-year-old male presented with a one-year history of progressive difficulty walking, declining balance, and neuropathic pain in his extremities. He was graded Nurick grade 3 and modified Japanese Orthopaedic Association (mJOA) score of 15. Cervical MRI showed severe cervical stenosis from C2-C3 to C5-C6 with associated hyperintense intramedullary signal change at C5-C6.
resident.physical_exam: Temperature 36°C, blood pressure 189/96 mmHg, heart rate 54 bpm. Physical examination notable for decreased cervical range of motion because of pain. The patient exhibited 5/5 strength in all muscle groups of the upper and lower extremities except for 4/5 strength in bilateral biceps and triceps. Sensation to light touch was decreased in bilateral upper and lower extremities. Bilateral upper and lower extremities revealed hyperreflexia.
key_positive_signs: 4/5 strength in bilateral biceps and triceps
Decreased sensation to light touch in bilateral upper and lower extremities
Bilateral upper and lower extremity hyperreflexia
Decreased cervical range of motion due to pain
resident.past_history: 15 pack-year smoking history, poorly controlled hypertension, medications metoprolol tartrate 25 mg twice daily and oxycodone 20 mg twice daily, remote lumbar transforaminal interbody fusion in 2001.
resident.public_message: This is a 63-year-old male with a one-year history of progressive difficulty walking, declining balance, and neuropathic extremity pain (Nurick grade 3, mJOA 15). Cervical MRI demonstrated severe stenosis from C2-C3 to C5-C6 with T2 hyperintense signal change at C5-C6. Past medical history includes a 15 pack-year smoking history, poorly controlled hypertension, medications metoprolol tartrate 25 mg BID and oxycodone 20 mg BID, and remote lumbar transforaminal interbody fusion in 2001. Vital signs: temperature 36°C, blood pressure 189/96 mmHg, heart rate 54 bpm. Physical exam showed decreased cervical range of motion due to pain, 4/5 strength in bilateral biceps and triceps (otherwise 5/5), decreased light touch sensation bilaterally, and bilateral hyperreflexia. Hemoglobin 15 g/dL.

imaging.public_message: Reporting the case record's description of the imaging; the films were not available for review. The record describes severe cervical stenosis from C2-3 through C5-6, with associated hyperintense intramedullary cord signal change at C5-6. The direction of compression is not stated. These findings correlate highly with the reported progressive myelopathic symptoms.

neurology.localization: Cervical myelopathy, with the lesion most consistent with the cervical spinal cord at C5-C6 given the intramedullary signal change and bilateral upper extremity weakness plus hyperreflexia; the hyperreflexia in all four limbs localizes to the upper motor neuron pathways above C5.

red_flags.finding: Remote lumbar transforaminal interbody fusion (2001) with reported lower extremity symptoms.
red_flags.rationale: Does not explain the upper extremity hyperreflexia or weakness, and the lower extremity upper motor neuron signs are readily attributed to the cervical lesion; no evidence of active lumbar pathology is provided, so it does not change the indication or plan.

red_flags.finding: Neuropathic pain in all extremities and symmetric decreased light touch sensation, without a documented sensory level or peripheral nerve examination.
red_flags.rationale: These features could suggest a coexisting peripheral neuropathy or central sensitization, but the presence of hyperreflexia and upper motor neuron signs indicates that cervical cord compression is the dominant cause of the myelopathic syndrome. This does not change the indication for addressing the cervical stenosis, though further electrodiagnostic testing could be considered if symptoms persist or confound assessment.

neurology.public_message: The examination localizes to the cervical spinal cord: bilateral upper and lower extremity hyperreflexia, bilateral biceps/triceps weakness, and gait difficulty are consistent with a cervical myelopathy, and the MRI findings of severe stenosis from C2-C3 to C5-C6 with cord signal change at C5-C6 explain the dominant syndrome (match level high). Two coexisting findings are noted: (1) the remote lumbar fusion does not alter the cervical localization or plan, and (2) the neuropathic pain and symmetric sensory loss raise the possibility of a coexisting peripheral neuropathy or central sensitization, but they do not change the indication for addressing the cervical stenosis because hyperreflexia indicates central nervous system involvement.

anesthesia.public_message: ASA grade III. Intraoperative mean arterial pressure target 85 mmHg. Blood loss risk: moderate. Extubation difficulty: unassessable because no formal airway assessment is recorded. Prone position tolerance: moderate.

physiatrist_opening.proposed_duration: 3 months of structured conservative management, with reassessment every 6 weeks
preconditions_for_failure: Worsening of myelopathic signs: decline in mJOA score by 2 or more points, new bowel or bladder dysfunction, or new motor weakness
Progression of gait impairment or falls
New or worsening cervical cord signal change on follow-up MRI
Intractable neuropathic pain unresponsive to conservative measures
Failure to show stabilization or improvement by 3 months
physiatrist_opening.public_message: While severe cervical stenosis with cord signal change and progressive myelopathy is concerning, I propose a time-limited trial of structured conservative management before surgery. The patient's deficits, though significant, have not shown acute deterioration, and surgery carries non-negligible risk given his poorly controlled hypertension and smoking history. A 3-month program of physical therapy, pain management, strict activity modification, and close monitoring is a reasonable first step. I estimate the conservative success rate in this specific presentation at approximately 10%—low but not zero—and therefore I cannot yet concede that surgery is the only option. The preconditions for declaring conservative failure are explicit: any worsening of myelopathic signs, new gait or balance decline, or intractable pain would trigger immediate surgical referral. Until those criteria are met, I maintain my stance for conservative care.

physiatrist_final.public_message: Director, to answer your question directly: I would agree to immediate surgery rather than a 3-month conservative trial only if the following conditions are present at baseline: (1) acute or rapidly progressive myelopathy (defined as a decline of 2 or more points on mJOA within 4 weeks), (2) new bowel or bladder dysfunction of cord origin, (3) imaging demonstrates severe cord compression with T2 hyperintense signal change plus evidence of myelomalacia or cystic change that portends imminent irreversible injury, or (4) inability to safely control blood pressure for surgery within a reasonable timeframe. None of these are documented in the record. The Deputy Director points to the cord signal change and the gradual progression as reasons to avoid delay, but I have already incorporated both into my 10% success estimate and my explicit failure criteria; the very gradual nature of the progression, without acute deterioration, supports that a closely monitored 3-month trial would detect worsening early enough to proceed to surgery without materially increasing risk of irreversible cord damage. Therefore, I maintain that a time-limited conservative trial remains a reasonable option before committing this patient to surgery.

vice_opinions.assessment: This is a 63-year-old man with progressive cervical myelopathy (Nurick grade 3, mJOA 15) caused by severe multi-level cervical stenosis from C2-C3 to C5-C6 with cord signal change at C5-C6. The clinical picture is consistent and surgical decompression is indicated; conservative management carries a high risk of irreversible neurological decline, and I do not support a trial of non-operative care. The patient's poorly controlled hypertension and smoking status require optimization but do not change the indication for surgery. The exact surgical approach depends on review of the actual imaging, particularly the direction of cord compression and sagittal alignment.
proposed_options: Posterior cervical laminectomy and instrumented fusion C2-C6
Posterior cervical laminoplasty C3-C6 (if lordosis is preserved and compression is dorsal)
Multilevel anterior cervical decompression and fusion (if compression is predominantly ventral and feasible)
vice_opinions.preferred_option: Posterior cervical laminectomy and instrumented fusion C2-C6
disagreement_points: I disagree with the physiatry suggestion of a 3-month conservative trial. Progressive myelopathy with cord signal change is a surgical indication, and delay risks further cord damage.

The imaging report does not state whether the compression is ventral, dorsal, or circumferential, and no sagittal alignment is given; this information is required to finalize the surgical approach, and I consider it an open contested question rather than a settled detail.
deferred_questions_to_director: After you review the imaging, do you agree with a posterior decompression and fusion, or would you consider an anterior approach?
Should we include C2-C3 in the decompression and fusion construct, or is the clinically significant stenosis more localized?
What preoperative blood pressure control is required before we schedule surgery, and can that be managed while booking the case?
vice_opinions.public_message: I agree that this is progressive cervical myelopathy with clear surgical indication. I do not support a conservative trial—the risk of irreversible deterioration outweighs the modest benefits of surgery, and the physiatry estimate of 10% success is not enough to justify delay. My preference is posterior cervical laminectomy and instrumented fusion from C2 to C6, pending review of the actual MRI to confirm the direction of compression and sagittal alignment. I have two open questions for the director: first, whether to include C2-C3 in the construct after seeing the films; second, what blood pressure target we must achieve before proceeding to the operating room.

director_rulings.public_message: Thank you all. I hear a genuine disagreement between Dr. Physiatrist and Dr. Deputy Director, with the neurologist and radiologist supporting surgery. My current view is that surgery is indicated for this progressive myelopathy with cord signal change. I am not yet ready to rule because the actual imaging is not available to confirm direction of compression and sagittal alignment, and blood pressure control needs to be addressed. I am ordering the following tests: formal radiologist review of the original MRI with specific reporting on compression direction and alignment, and flexion-extension and standing cervical radiographs. I ask Dr. Resident to obtain those films and Dr. Radiologist to report on the direction of compression and whether a posterior approach is adequate. I ask Dr. Anesthesiologist to specify the precise preoperative blood pressure target and the maximum acceptable delay to achieve it. I ask Dr. Physiatrist to state under what exact conditions he would agree to immediate surgery rather than a 3-month trial, given his 10% estimate. I acknowledge the Deputy Director's objection that the imaging does not state compression direction or sagittal alignment; this objection has merit, and our surgical approach will be revised accordingly once the imaging is reviewed. If the MRI review reveals predominantly ventral compression, the surgical plan will shift to an anterior approach; if blood pressure cannot be optimized within a reasonable timeframe, surgery will be deferred until control is achieved. We will reconvene after these results are available.

director_rulings.final_decision: Surgery is indicated for this progressive cervical myelopathy with cord signal change. I reject the proposed 3-month conservative trial: the 10% estimated success does not justify the risk of irreversible cord injury, and the physiatrist's preconditions for immediate surgery would dangerously delay treatment. Before proceeding, we must complete the imaging review to determine the direction of compression and sagittal alignment, and achieve acceptable blood pressure control. Therefore, I am closing this meeting on the instruction that the following workup be completed first, after which we reconvene to finalize the surgical plan. If the MRI review confirms dorsal or neutral compression with preserved sagittal alignment, we will proceed with posterior laminectomy and instrumented fusion from C2 to C6. If ventral compression is predominant, the plan will shift to an anterior approach. Explicit imaging criteria for including C2-C3 in the construct are: severe stenosis (>50% canal compromise) at C2-C3, dynamic instability on flexion-extension (>3 mm translation or >11° segmental angulation), or segmental kyphosis. For blood pressure, the anesthesiologist will specify a target (mean arterial pressure 85 mmHg) and the maximum acceptable delay to achieve it; if control cannot be achieved within that timeframe, surgery will be deferred until it is.
